messages.body_plain:
Hi there,
I am a new user in this field and facing some issues with some analysis.

I did an analysis of how the shape changes with different population types before and after allometry correction. But I got comments from one of my reviewers as below:

"Before correcting for allometry in this manner you need to confirm that your groups share a common allometric trajectory. Essentially this is a test of Coords ~ Size*Type. If the interaction is significant, groups do not share common slopes and instead, you need to compare the different allometric trajectories rather than correcting for common allometry. If that interaction is not significant then you can proceed with allometry correcting as you did."

I ran the following code-
> fullmodsize2 <- procD.lm(dat2$coords ~ Csize*poptype + Csize*poptype/site, data = geodf)
> anova(fullmodsize2)
> plot(fullmodsize2, size = dat2$Csize, logsz = TRUE, type = "regression", reg.type = "PredLine", predictor = log(geodf$Csize), pch = 19, col = as.numeric(geodf$poptype))

                    Df      SS       MS     Rsq       F       Z Pr(>F)
Csize                1 0.04776 0.047760 0.09325 66.0244  9.2061  0.001 **
poptype              2 0.06324 0.031620 0.12347 43.7119 11.7981  0.001 **
Csize:poptype        2 0.01093 0.005467 0.02135  7.5577  6.9040  0.001 **
Csize:poptype:site  14 0.07343 0.005245 0.14336  7.2505 15.7210  0.001 **
Residuals          438 0.31684 0.000723 0.61858
Total              457 0.51220
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

This interaction seems significant, but my question is which interaction gives more appropriate results from the following to test that:
 > fullmodsize2 <- procD.lm(dat2$coords ~ Csize*poptype + Csize*poptype/site, data = geodf                       or,
> fullmodsize1 <- procD.lm(dat2$coords ~ Csize * poptype + poptype/site, data = geodf)  or,
> allo.unique <- procD.lm(dat2$coords ~ Csize * poptype/site, iter = 99, RRPP=TRUE, data = geodf)  or,
> allo.common <- procD.lm(dat2$coords ~ Csize + poptype/site, iter = 99, RRPP=TRUE, data = geodf)

Later, I compared the different allometric trajectories. First, I looked at how the shape changes at min and max sizes by using shape.predictor as follows-

> preds <- shape.predictor(dat2$coords, x= log(dat2$Csize), Intercept = TRUE, predmin =  min(log(dat2$Csize)), predmax = max(log(dat2$Csize)))
> plotRefToTarget(mshape(dat2$coords), preds$predmin, mag=1.5)
> plotRefToTarget(mshape(dat2$coords), preds$predmax, mag=1.5)

I also compared the allometric trajectories in different size ranges.
> preds1 <- shape.predictor(dat2$coords, x= log(dat2$Csize), Intercept = TRUE, method = "PLS", pred2 = 2.4, pred3 = 2.2, pred4 = 2.4, pred5 = 2.6, pred6 = 2.8, pred7 = 3.0)
> plotRefToTarget(mshape(dat2$coords), preds1$pred2, mag=0.5)
> plotRefToTarget(mshape(dat2$coords), preds1$pred3, mag=0.5)
> plotRefToTarget(mshape(dat2$coords), preds1$pred4, mag=0.5)
> plotRefToTarget(mshape(dat2$coords), preds1$pred5, mag=0.5)
> plotRefToTarget(mshape(dat2$coords), preds1$pred6, mag=0.5)
> plotRefToTarget(mshape(dat2$coords), preds1$pred7, mag=0.5)

But is there any way of comparing the shape of a particular size (min and max maybe) for different population types? Above all gives me a grid of common body shape changes. But I want to have three different grid plots for the different population types.

I also did the pairwise comparisons. Does the below trajectories analysis worth doing?
> TA <- trajectory.analysis(fullmodesize2, groups = geodf$poptype, traj.pts = geodf$site, pca = TRUE, print.progress = FALSE)
> summary(TA, attribute = "SD")
> TP <- plot(TA, pch = 19, cex = 0.7, col = as.numeric(geodf$poptype))
add.trajectories(TP, traj.bg <http://traj.bg> = 1:nlevels(geodf$poptype), start.bg <http://start.bg> = 1:nlevels(geodf$poptype),end.bg <http://end.bg> = 1:nlevels(geodf$poptype))
> summary(TA, attribute = "SD") # SD= Shape differences trajectories
Trajectory analysis
100 permutations.
Points projected onto trajectory PCs
Trajectories:
Trajectories hidden (use show.trajectories = TRUE to view)

Pairwise trajectory shape differences, plus statistics
                                            d UCL (95%)           Z Pr > d
Chatham Coastal:Chatham Landlocked  0.4322844 0.6564523 -0.36006097  0.638
Chatham Coastal:Mainland Coastal    0.5334438 0.8297494 -1.81942906  0.958
Chatham Landlocked:Mainland Coastal 0.6159263 0.7787542 -0.04288519  0.515

Am I on the right track that the reviewers ask for?

Thanks in advance.

Kind regards,
Motia

Motia,

Your post had several components, and my response here addresses the main points related directly to the reviewer comments. First, your model of shape ~ Size*Pop finds a significant interaction with a large effect size. This means that the allometric trends across poptypes are not consistent, which then means that allometric ‘correction’ using a common slope is incorrect.

What the reviewer then requests is a comparison of slopes. This is done using the function ‘pairwise’ in RRPP: geomorph’s companion package.  If you look at the help file of that function, there is an example of comparing slopes. One fits the full model, uses pairwise, and then summarizes using test.type = “VC” (vector correlations). This is what the reviewer requested.

Your post then asked about what interaction gives a more significant result. That is harder to answer, as there is both a conceptual and a statistical component to the question. My first question would be: what is the most appropriate model to be using given your data, your biological design, etc. That should dictate analytical procedure more than which model is more ‘significant’. To me this seems more ancillary to the reviewer’s question.

Hope this helps.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph-ers,

I'm looking for advice on the latest methods to identify unknown specimens using GM. Let's say I have landmark data for ~300 skulls, many of them with associated genomes. And now I want to place fossils (with no DNA) into that phylomorphospace to see who they fall closest to. What would be the best way to do that? DFA, CVA, Procrustes distance, nearest-neighbor distance? I understand for any of these that one would want to use the full trait space, not just e.g. PC1 & PC2.

Thanks for any suggestions and relevant literature.

Christy

Hi Christy,

A two-part response!  First, you could use the prep.lda function in RRPP, using either a procD.lm or lm.rrpp fit.  This is the same as CVA or DFA (lda means linear discriminant analysis), but as an advantage to the typically limited applications of these techniques, prep.lda allows one to use other covariates and factors in the model rather than just “group”.  Additionally, one can use training data and test data, plus ascribed prior probabilities to calculate posterior probabilities in a Bayesian framework.  The prep.lda help file shows how to set up an analysis for the lda function (and that help file can take you the rest of the way).  It’s pretty slick, and you can find confidence intervals for probabilities of group association, rather than just a binary yes/no for classification.

You should use data that does not contain a specimen to train the model and use the specimen’s data as test data (this can be done with the predict.lda function).  However, and this is the second part, I might argue that there is no way to have truly independent training and test data when the data is produced from a generalized Procrustes Analysis, as the one specimen used as test data is still used in GPA, and thus, has some contribution to the superimposition.  This is less worry with sufficiently large data sets but could be a concern for small data sets.  With a small data set, one might want to first do GPA without the specimen, get the consensus configuration, and align the one specimen, adjusted to unit size, to the mean, to use as data obtained independent of the GPA but still aligned to the GPA.  This is more involved but manageable.

Hope that helps!
Mike

I suppose in my case one could use some factor of genotype as groups, or even some continuous variable describing ancestry (in my case, this would be proportion wolf vs dog ancestry). On Friday, August 12, 2022 at 4:29:33 PM UTC+2 mlco...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Christy,
>
> A two-part response!  First, you could use the prep.lda function in RRPP, using either a procD.lm or lm.rrpp fit.  This is the same as CVA or DFA (lda means linear discriminant analysis), but as an advantage to the typically limited applications of these techniques, prep.lda allows one to use other covariates and factors in the model rather than just “group”.  Additionally, one can use training data and test data, plus ascribed prior probabilities to calculate posterior probabilities in a Bayesian framework.  The prep.lda help file shows how to set up an analysis for the lda function (and that help file can take you the rest of the way).  It’s pretty slick, and you can find confidence intervals for probabilities of group association, rather than just a binary yes/no for classification.
>
> You should use data that does not contain a specimen to train the model and use the specimen’s data as test data (this can be done with the predict.lda function).  However, and this is the second part, I might argue that there is no way to have truly independent training and test data when the data is produced from a generalized Procrustes Analysis, as the one specimen used as test data is still used in GPA, and thus, has some contribution to the superimposition.  This is less worry with sufficiently large data sets but could be a concern for small data sets.  With a small data set, one might want to first do GPA without the specimen, get the consensus configuration, and align the one specimen, adjusted to unit size, to the mean, to use as data obtained independent of the GPA but still aligned to the GPA.  This is more involved but manageable.
>
> Hope that helps!
> Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ashly,

If your analysis is for object symmetry, there is no Csize output, but you could just perform GPA with gpagen and you will have Csize as output for the each specimen's entire configuration.  If you analysis is for matching symmetry, You could either perform GPA separately (there is an example in the help file how to run bilat.syymetry on a gpagen object, in which case you have Csize already form the gpagen object) or you can extract Csize indirectly from the $procD.lm.size$data output of the bilat.symmetry object.  Keep in mind you will have two or more centroid sizes for each specimen, so you would have to contrive a way to summarize them.

Because an arbitrary choice must be made for how to summarize multiple centroid sizes per specimen (for matching symmetry), providing a full-specimen centroid size as output would mean asserting an arbitrary choice as appropriate, which (in my opinion) exceeds the scope of the bilat.symmetry analysis, and good reason not to include any centroid size output, other than for the matching configuration replicates (which it does already).

Hope that helps!
Mike

I did not know that MorphoJ attempts to provide one centroid size for replicated configurations. I assume that the program finds the mean of configurations, unless otherwise stated in the documentation. Taking either the mean or the sum — assuming each specimen’s configuration is replicated the same number of times — would have the same ANOVA outcome when regressing individual asymmetry versus size.

In case it helps, the simplest way to do this in R, for a gpagen object called GPA and a vector of specimen names called id is:

CombCsize <- by(GPA$Csize, id, mean)

Or

CombCsize <- by(GPA$Csize, id, sum)

You might also need to use as.vector to remove unneeded formatting before analysis.

Cheers!
Mike

Dear Agnese,

Hear is the textbook definition.  Coefficients are scalars that express the expected per unit changes in a set of dependent or response variables, based on the parameters of a linear model design matrix.  In this case there are 24 dependent variables (Procrustes residuals) and 5 parameters required for the three independent variables and the interaction between two of them.  I suspect that your question does not seek the textbook definition as much as it seeks the understanding you might attain from thorough reading of a linear models textbook.  There is no way to overcome that in a few sentences.  In my opinion, working with geometric morphometrics requires some training in linear models.  Virtually all analyses in geometric morphometrics, or in statistics for that matter, are based on linear models.  (Most introductory statistics courses do not include a teaching of linear models, which is unfortunate, in my opinion.)  I suspect that any formal training in geometric morphometrics also includes training in linear models.  (Any workshop for which I have been involved as participant or instructor has.)  If the terms “linear model design matrix” or “coefficients” do not have clear meaning, it probably means one’s training in linear models is limited, and I recommend remedying that more than attempting to understand geometric morphometrics without this training.

In terms of coefficient labels in R, they match linear model design matrix parameters (columns), which includes an intercept.  One can deduce that the intercept corresponds to estimation of shapes for allopatric Plethodon jordani, because “speciesTayah" means the expected amount of shape change if a species in Plethodon teyahalee and “siteSymp” means the expected amount of shape change if the specimen is from a sympatric site.  The first part of each term (e.g., species) is the variable name and the second part is the level of variable being changed (e.g., Teyah”).  By process of elimination, neither Jord nor Allo are listed as coefficients, so these must be the starting conditions (the intercept).  Again, if this explanation does not seem to make much sense, it probably means a limited understanding of linear model designs rather than R’s way of identifying coefficients.

Here is a good linear models source:

Rencher, A. C., & Schaalje, G. B. (2008). Linear models in statistics. John Wiley & Sons.

I believe there are pirated copies on the internet.

hope this helps.

Mike

Hi all,

I'm fairly new to geomorph and I'm trying to wrap my head around the significance of my data. I'll try to sketch the situation:

I have 182 samples of landmarked data (22 landmarks each), of which 13 species are 'outgroups' (ingroup is therefore 169). I made morphospaces of both datasets (ingroup separately, and ingroup + outgroup combined), and labelled the points based on the species' host-association. I want to know if the mean shapes of these points clouds (convex hulls) are significant different from one-another. Therefore I did a pairwise Procrustes ANOVA using the following script:

Procrustes <- gpagen(mydata, curves = slider_matrix)
y<-two.d.array(Procrustes$coords)
x<-as.factor(df$V4) #df is the dataframe, V4 is the host-association
Procrustes_anova <- procD.lm(y~x)
summary(Procrustes_anova)
PW <- pairwise(Procrustes_anova, groups = x, covariate = NULL)
summary(PW, show.vectors = TRUE, test.type = "dist")

In the morphospace with only the ingroup included, almost all groups were found to be siginificantly different (P <0.05), although the point clouds are all overlapping and barely any visual differences in the mean shapes were seen when performing plotRefToTarget.
In the morphospace including the outgroups, which are outside of the overlapping point cloud, the P-values go up. Even in the comparison of clouds which (almost; due to new Procrustes superimpositioning) stay the same, the p-values change a lot.

So my question here is:
Am I doing this correct, and is the pairwise test using relative distances in the entire morphospace to seek for significance?
And when searching for an answer I found a lot of users use a disparity test to find between-group differences. How is this different from my current analysis? If I use morphol.disparity(Procrustes$coords ~ 1, groups = x), I get insiginificant values for all groups except for the outgroup - is disparity here a proxy for overlapping in the morphospace?
Thanks in advance, really appreciate it!

Best wishes, and groetjes from the Netherlands,
Werner de Gier

Werner,

several points here:

1. Yes, your general approach for testing for group differences is correct
2. Keep in mind that p-values using a procD.lm anova is based on permutation of residuals (for more on this please see the RRPP package and corresponding papers). This means that if you change your sample (ingroup vs. ingroup+ougroup) the available data for running permutations change and as such p-values are also bound to change.
3. I am guessing that when looking at "overlap" of groups you are doing so in a PCA space. Keep in mind that this is a reduction of the total shape space on which ANOVA and pairwise comparisons are being run. As such, what you see "by eye" does not necessarily fully express the ANOVA tests. A PCA seeks general variation in your sample, which does not need to align with differentiation between groups (which is what ANOVA is looking at). Trust stats first, and then use a PCA to illustrate and explore patterns, would be my suggestion.
4. Kind of the same goes for deformation grids. If you KNOW (from your stats) that there are significant differences between your groups, and want to visualize those, go ahead and exaggerate shape differences using the mag argument in plotRefToTarget. Remember to say that you did so in the legend of your paper figure. If no significant differences exist, deformation grids are just a mathematical construct and not informative.
5. ANOVAs test for differences in mean shape among groups (and pairwise comparisons investigate which groups differ). As is the case for any ANOVA, this is done taking group dispersion into account (are differences between groups large enough in comparison to variation within groups?). Disparity analysis does a whole different thing, i.e. it tests for differences in the multivariate dispersion of your groups NOT their mean shapes. Depending on your biological question this can be informative, e.g. as to sources of morphological variation etc. I recommend you carefully read the help page of that function and corresponding cited papers for that, as it is an entire investigation field within morphometrics.

Hope this helps
Antigoni

> 3. I am guessing that when looking at "overlap" of groups you are doing so in a PCA space. Keep in mind that this is a reduction of the total shape space on which ANOVA and pairwise comparisons are being run. As such, what you see "by eye" does not necessarily fully express the ANOVA tests. A PCA seeks general variation in your sample, which does not need to align with differentiation between groups (which is what ANOVA is looking at). Trust stats first, and then use a PCA to illustrate and explore patterns, would be my suggestion.
> 4. Kind of the same goes for deformation grids. If you KNOW (from your stats) that there are significant differences between your groups, and want to visualize those, go ahead and exaggerate shape differences using the mag argument in plotRefToTarget. Remember to say that you did so in the legend of your paper figure. If no significant differences exist, deformation grids are just a mathematical construct and not informative.
> 5. ANOVAs test for differences in mean shape among groups (and pairwise comparisons investigate which groups differ). As is the case for any ANOVA, this is done taking group dispersion into account (are differences between groups large enough in comparison to variation within groups?). Disparity analysis does a whole different thing, i.e. it tests for differences in the multivariate dispersion of your groups NOT their mean shapes. Depending on your biological question this can be informative, e.g. as to sources of morphological variation etc. I recommend you carefully read the help page of that function and corresponding cited papers for that, as it is an entire investigation field within morphometrics.
